taxonomic_note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO. Kew treats Eragrostis intermedia var. appressa and Eragrostis lugens var. major as synonyms of the species; learner remains species-level.
look_here_first: First read the open, airy, broadly ovate mature panicle. Then inspect the sheath SURFACE and the sheath throat: typically rather smooth away from the apex, with conspicuous throat/collar hairs. Check several panicle branch junctions; occasional axil hairs do not make this E. hirsuta. Confirm from mature spikelets and local key, not color alone.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Kew/POWO accepts E. intermedia and lists Texas in its native range. Hagenbuch & Lemke's Texas Hill Country grass treatment cites multiple Hays County specimens (Breckenridge 457, Jessup 57, Lemke 674, Lyday 281, Ruiseco 11). The same treatment cites Gillespie County specimen Sanchez 960. The same treatment cites Val Verde County specimens Labus 129 and 197; it also cites a Bandera/Medina County collection.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: County PASS is based on cited herbarium vouchers in a regional grass treatment, not broad ecoregion presence or seeded roadside/landscape occurrences.

best_field_traits: perennial, caespitose/tufted grass with erect culms commonly around 30–75 cm
leaves basal and cauline; blades narrow, roughly 1–5 mm wide
leaf sheaths mostly glabrous to only sparsely papillose, with hairs near the apex/collar
ligule a very short fringe/line of hairs
panicle very open and broadly ovoid, often occupying a large fraction of plant height
panicle branch axils only sparsely hairy, especially at lower nodes
primary panicle branches bare for a distance near their bases
pedicels mostly much longer than the small spikelets and divergent
spikelets small, green to purple-tinged, generally with only a few florets
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Eragrostis hirsuta: Bigtop lovegrass is conspicuously hairier: its leaf sheaths are hirsute and panicle branch axils are bearded. It is commonly taller with a larger panicle. E. intermedia has mostly smooth sheaths and only sparse axillary hairs. Eragrostis trichodes: Sand lovegrass often shows conspicuous long hair tufts at the sheath apex/collar and a taller, narrow-based plant with a large diffuse panicle; use sheath/collar hair placement and spikelet/panicle architecture rather than overall airiness alone. Eragrostis cilianensis: Stinkgrass is an annual with a much coarser, denser-looking panicle and gland-dotted lemmas; crushed young plants may have a strong odor. It is introduced in Texas.
crew_field_walkthrough: 1. FROM A FEW FEET AWAY: photograph the whole rooted tuft plus the ENTIRE open, broadly oval panicle. An airy panicle is an entry clue, not a species-level ID.

2. AT THE LEAF: peel one mature blade outward to expose the sheath mouth, collar and hair-fringed ligule. Photograph whether the long hairs are mostly concentrated at the throat/apex rather than uniformly shaggy over the sheath.
3. AT THE PANICLE: photograph several branch junctions, especially the lower ones. E. intermedia may have hairs at lower branch axils; do NOT treat 'any bearded axil' as automatic E. hirsuta.

4. AT THE SPIKELET: use a millimeter scale and magnification. Record spikelet length, approximate floret count, relative glume length, and whether pedicels are long or short across several mature branches.

5. COMPARE: E. hirsuta favors conspicuously hairy sheaths throughout and prominently bearded branch axils. E. trichodes often has larger, more elongate panicles with conspicuous sheath-mouth hair tufts. If the sheath, spikelets or mature head are missing, leave the field ID at Eragrostis sp.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Whole plant with basal tuft visible and a complete mature panicle in frame; place ruler beside inflorescence.
Undisturbed leaf sheath surface AND an extreme close view of the collar/ligule; document where hairs actually originate.
Two or more lower panicle branch axils; confirm whether hairs arise in a tuft and whether the rest of the branch is hairy.
Multiple mature spikelets at scale, showing glumes and number of florets; isolate one without mixing parts from adjacent spikelets.
A matched same-day look-alike, especially E. hirsuta or E. trichodes, photographed with the same views for a genuine side-by-side comparison.
field_identification_cautions: Purple hue and general airy-panicle appearance overlap among several local lovegrasses.

Some published descriptions disagree on pedicel-to-spikelet length and typical floret number. Do not build a yes/no key from either alone until source concepts and locally vouchered specimens are reconciled.
Hairs at the panicle branch axils are not unique to E. hirsuta; distinguish diffuse sheath hairiness from a few localized tufts.
Do not infer a finished diagnostic photo, a measured structure or an accurate arrow from an image filename or role caption. Validate the actual pixels.

comparisons.key_distinctions: E. hirsuta usually has more conspicuous hairs on the sheath surface/margins and bearded panicle axils; E. trichodes commonly has a taller, elongated diffuse panicle and long hairs concentrated at the sheath throat, with spikelets sometimes near branch tips. E. spectabilis can make an exceptionally broad loose purple tumbleweed-like panicle. Witchgrass (Panicum capillare) has a different spikelet construction; dissect before using color or openness.

field_id_finish_pass.looked_at: Existing credited Joey Santore local photos: whole rocky-site clump, hand-held open panicle, and intact seedhead. Photo pixels examined 2026-10-20; no visible collar or measured mature spikelets in these photos.
field_id_finish_pass.crew_summary: Plains lovegrass often looks like a loose, nearly transparent branching cloud over a grass tuft. Ask the crew to find the sheath/collar before separating it from other airy lovegrasses.
lookalike_logic: Bigtop: test sheath hairiness along the sheath body and bearded panicle axils.
Sand: inspect comparatively elongated panicle, throat hairs and spikelet placement.
Purple lovegrass: very broadly spread flexible panicle, often much more showy/tumbleweed-like.
Witchgrass: grass panicle silhouette can overlap, but reproductive spikelet structure differs.
difficult_id_guardrails: Sheath hair placement requires a real collar view; none of these three inspected images provides it.
Texas A&M and FNA-linked treatments differ on pedicel-to-spikelet ratios and floret descriptions; do not teach those as absolute photo-alone splits.
No new local range certification was performed; preserve accepted taxon and county evidence.
The source observation identification is not a specimen-level independent expert redetermination.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Plains lovegrass: don't stop at the airy panicle
steps: Find a true branched panicle and a few tiny separate spikelets on thin branches; use the hand-held photographs as shape references.
Inspect the sheath BODY versus throat/collar under 10×: E. intermedia is usually less hairy along the sheath surface than bigtop lovegrass.
Check at least two lower panicle branch junctions and mature spikelets; compare with E. hirsuta and E. trichodes before deciding.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Panicle openness alone is a hint. Without sheath and mature spikelet macro, keep Eragrostis sp.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: No collar, ligule, sheath-surface or measured floret photo is yet locked in this card. The visible arrows only mark macro architecture, NOT microscopic proof.
